title: Build
content:
vendor/bin/wp-app-framework build [--output=<file>]

Builds and checks the manifest of the project whose vendor/autoload.php the Composer bin proxy loads; problems are listed with class and parameter names, and the exit code is 1. Without --output nothing is written; a written manifest is a release manifest and carries the template version. Do not write generated/manifest.php into a source checkout of a theme or plugin: its presence selects release mode (see Boot and modes). The release build writes it.

title: Releases and CI
content:
Repositories are released by tags v<semantic version>; GitHub Actions run the release pipeline and attach the artifact to the GitHub release of the tag, only after it passed its tests.

Themes, child themes and plugins

They call the reusable workflow .github/workflows/consumer-release.yml of the framework repository from a workflow on push: tags: ['v*'] with permissions: contents: write (see theme-dev-test, theme-dev-test-child and plugin-dev-test).

The workflow:

checks out the project and wp-dev-env,

runs composer lint and npm run lint (if defined) and wp-app-framework build,

builds the release with --expect-version of the tag,

installs the ZIP into a plain WordPress (scripts/release-test),

runs the project's browser tests (npm run test:e2e, with E2E_TARGET=release; input e2e: false skips them).

The type in composer.json and the Template: header of style.css decide how the ZIP is installed; a plugin is installed next to the release ZIP of a theme, a child theme on top of the release ZIP of its parent theme, given as input with-theme: <owner>/<repository>@<tag> (required for plugins and child themes).

Inputs: repository, ref, e2e, publish, framework-ref, wp-dev-env-ref, with-theme. Consumers pin the workflow to a framework tag.

The framework

ci.yml runs PHPUnit, Vitest and all linters on pushes and pull requests, and builds this documentation.

release.yml runs them for a tag, then the release gates – theme-dev-test, plugin-dev-test and theme-dev-test-child built with the framework of the tag (framework-ref) and tested in the browser, the plugin and the child theme with an older release of the theme, without publishing – and finally attaches wp-app-framework-<version>.zip (git archive, without the export-ignore development files) to the GitHub release and publishes the documentation of the tag's minor version.

Requiring the framework

Themes require the framework from its repository by version; the lock file pins the commit:

"repositories": [{"type": "vcs", "url": "https://github.com/saijsaij/wp-app-framework"}]
description: Repositories are released by tags v<semantic version>; GitHub Actions run the release pipeline and attach the artifact to the GitHub release of the tag, only after it passed its tests.

title: Release
content:
vendor/bin/wp-app-framework release [--output=<zip>] [--expect-version=<version>] [--package-source=<package>=<directory>]...

Builds the release ZIP of a theme or plugin (by the type in its composer.json) – plain WordPress needs no Composer: all dependencies, including this framework and Twig, ship prefixed in vendor-prefixed/, so several consumers with different framework versions coexist. The command works on a copy in the system's temporary directory and never changes the checkout:

Copies the files git does not ignore (git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard, so uncommitted changes are included). generated/manifest.php must not exist in the checkout.

composer install --no-dev --classmap-authoritative from the lock file. --package-source=saij/wp-app-framework=../wp-app-framework replaces a package by a copy of a local checkout (its files without export-ignore, like a distribution archive), e.g. to test unreleased framework changes; the output says that the build is not from the lock file. Path repositories are not supported: the copy has no sibling checkouts.

Runs Strauss (strauss in the PATH; the tools image of wp-dev-env provides it) with the call sites of the project, then patches Twig: Twig's compiler writes class names such as use Twig\Environment; as plain strings into every compiled template, which no prefixing tool rewrites. Release\TwigPatcher rewrites exactly these places and requires each pattern as often as expected, so a Twig update that changes them fails the build.

Builds generated/manifest.php with the prefixed classes (bin/wp-app-framework-prefixed.php in the prefixed copy, written with the template version), then compiles all templates of the project and the framework as release mode would and checks the compiled code for unprefixed names.

npm ci && npm run build (if there is a package.json), which builds the editor runtime from vendor/.

Removes node_modules/, vendor/, composer.json, composer.lock, package.json, package-lock.json and every path the project marks export-ignore in .gitattributes (use dir/** for directories), then checks all PHP files for names of dependencies that were not prefixed (string literals too, except inside vendor-prefixed/, where dependencies mention their own class names in messages).

Writes dist/<slug>-<version>.zip (or --output) with the project directory as root; slug = directory name, version = Version: of the (child) theme's style.css or of the plugin's main file <slug>.php, which --expect-version must match. A child theme is built without its parent theme: calls of the parent's public template callables compile without it.

Every step fails with the file, command or setting at fault; on failure the build directory is kept and its path printed.

Strauss settings

The project declares the Strauss settings in its composer.json – extra is part of the lock file's content hash, so the build cannot add them – and the command checks the values it relies on:

"extra": {
    "strauss": {
        "target_directory": "vendor-prefixed",
        "namespace_prefix": "Vendor\\Theme\\Vendor\\",
        "classmap_prefix": "Vendor_Theme_Vendor_",
        "include_root_autoload": true,
        "update_call_sites": ["src", "functions.php"],
        "delete_vendor_packages": false
    }
}

update_call_sites must contain the file that boots the framework (functions.php of a theme or child theme, <slug>.php of a plugin). The prefix must not be the project's own namespace (Strauss' default). Leave constant_prefix unset: it would rename the constants the Symfony polyfills define for PHP itself (e.g. MB_CASE_UPPER); Twig defines none.

Unreleased framework changes

To test a release with unreleased framework changes, run in the consumer:

composer release -- --package-source=saij/wp-app-framework=../wp-app-framework

title: Getting started
description: This page sets up a block theme my-theme with one block. Plugins and child themes with code of their own are set up the same way; see Boot and modes, Plugins and Child themes for the differences. You need PHP 8.5, Composer and Node 24 – or wp-dev-env, which provides them in a container together with a local WordPress.

title: Blocks
description: A block is a service class with #[Block] and a render() method; its attributes are a typed attribute class. There is no block.json: the build derives the attribute schema from the attribute class, and WordPress passes it to the editor (get_block_editor_server_block_settings()). The post content stores the block comment with the attributes as JSON, e.g. . The only markup in the post content is the value of a #[RichText(postContent: true)] field: inline HTML without wrapping element, e.g. Summer party (see Text in the post content). field(), inner_blocks() and is_editor() only matter in the editor; on the front end the marks are empty (see Editor).

title: Boot and modes
content:
Boot

The theme's functions.php loads the autoloader and boots the framework:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// Release builds ship prefixed dependencies in vendor-prefixed/; source checkouts use Composer's vendor/.
require is_file(__DIR__ . '/vendor-prefixed/autoload.php')
    ? __DIR__ . '/vendor-prefixed/autoload.php'
    : __DIR__ . '/vendor/autoload.php';

Saij\WpAppFramework\Theme::boot();

A plugin boots from its main file, which must be named after its directory (my-plugin/my-plugin.php):

<?php
/**
 * Plugin Name: My Plugin
 * Version: 1.0.0
 * Requires PHP: 8.5
 */

declare(strict_types=1);

require is_file(__DIR__ . '/vendor-prefixed/autoload.php')
    ? __DIR__ . '/vendor-prefixed/autoload.php'
    : __DIR__ . '/vendor/autoload.php';

Saij\WpAppFramework\Plugin::boot(__FILE__);

A child theme with code of its own (blocks, hooks, routes) boots its own framework instance from its functions.php, with the same autoloader lines and Saij\WpAppFramework\ChildTheme::boot(); – see Child themes. A child theme without code needs neither boot nor build.

The slug of a theme is get_template(), of a child theme get_stylesheet(), of a plugin its directory name; the asset URLs of a plugin come from plugin_dir_url(). Each slug boots once: a second boot with the same slug – from the same consumer, or a theme and a plugin with the same directory name – is an error. At its end, the boot fires the action wp_app_framework/init/{slug} (without arguments).

The type in the consumer's composer.json must be wordpress-theme or wordpress-plugin; the build reads the kind of the project from it. A theme needs a style.css; if it declares a parent theme (Template:), the project is a child theme.

Modes

Release mode: the theme or plugin contains generated/manifest.php, which only the release build creates. The manifest is loaded as is: no reflection, no file checks, no writes to the project. Compiled Twig templates go to a cache directory named after the template version of the release (see Twig templates).

Development mode: otherwise. The manifest is built by reflection and cached in wp-content/cache/{slug}/manifest/ (never in the project). Like Symfony's container cache in debug mode, a meta file records the resources the build depended on, using relative paths only. Each request compares modification times; only for newer files the class signature (attributes, parents, interfaces, traits and the signatures of the constructor and public methods, not method bodies) or file content is recomputed, and only a difference triggers a rebuild.
In development mode all consumers share the unprefixed classes of the framework and its dependencies: whichever autoloader comes first provides them. The boot therefore requires that the loaded framework is the consumer's own vendor/saij/wp-app-framework (by real path) and that the loaded Twig version is the one in its vendor/composer/installed.php, and fails otherwise. Link the same framework checkout into every consumer (WP_PACKAGE_LINKS of wp-dev-env).

title: Child themes
description: A child theme overrides templates of its parent theme in overrides/{parent-slug}/ (see Twig templates) and adjusts theme.json, block templates, template parts and patterns as WordPress allows; for that it needs no Composer, no boot and no build. A child theme with code of its own – blocks, hooks, REST routes – is a framework instance like a plugin: its own composer.json (type: wordpress-theme, its style.css names the parent theme in Template:), its own PSR-4 namespace and block namespace, its own release with its own prefix, and ChildTheme::boot() in its functions.php (see Boot and modes). WordPress loads that file before the parent theme's; the instances share nothing. The build records the parent theme in the manifest, and the boot fails if another parent theme is active. Block names that collide with the parent's are errors, as between any two instances. The child theme reaches its parent theme only through the parent's public interface (see Plugins): its public template callables, without declaring the parent, and its public API through a constructor parameter with #[ThemeApi] (Saij\WpAppFramework\Api\ThemeApi): The parent theme boots after the child theme, so the service must not be created before after_setup_theme. Require the parent theme as a development dependency for the IDE and static analysis. Child themes offer no public interface themselves.

title: Editor
content: The editor runtime renders every block of the theme or plugin in the block editor on the server, from the same Twig template as the front end, and replaces the marked elements with editors. Markup exists only once, in Twig. Templates In editor renders the template functions mark the editable elements: {{ field('topline') }}, {{ field('caption.text') }}, {{ field(['buttons', loop.index0, 'label']) }} on the element of an inline field. The path must name a #[PlainText], #[RichText] or #[Image] field of the block (list items by index); anything else throws an exception, in the editor and on the front end. Text fields become RichText with the element's tag; an image field keeps the server markup and offers select, replace and reset – mark an element around the image (e.g.

title: Hooks
description: The method must be public and non-static and declare a return type: void registers an action, any other type a filter. #[Hook] is repeatable.Parameters typed with a service candidate are injected (Formatter, see Services). All other parameters receive the WordPress arguments in their order ($title, $postId); accepted_args is derived from them. Missing optional arguments use the parameter default.Services are created when the hook fires. Exceptions are rethrown if WP_DEBUG is enabled; otherwise they are logged with error_log(), and filters return their original value.

title: Plugins
description: Plugins use the framework like themes (see Boot and modes) and may offer an interface to other consumers – the theme, other plugins. Themes may offer the same interface to their child themes. Instances never share PHP objects of the framework or of its dependencies: each release prefixes them with its own namespace. The interface therefore consists of WordPress hooks named after the provider's slug and of signatures that use only PHP, WordPress and the provider's own classes; the build of the provider rejects other types (also in the project classes such a signature uses). The provider keeps its interface compatible itself.

title: REST routes
Services
content:
Every concrete class under the consumer's PSR-4 directories (autoload.psr-4 in its composer.json) and under the framework's src/ is a service candidate. Interfaces, abstract classes, traits, enums, attribute classes and classes marked #[NoService] (Saij\WpAppFramework\DependencyInjection\NoService) are not. Services are shared and autowired by constructor parameter types; scalar parameters must have a default value.

Only services reachable from entry points (#[Hook], #[RestRoute], #[TemplateFunction] and #[TemplateFilter] methods, including permission callbacks, and #[Block] classes) are built and checked, so value objects that are never injected need no marking. Aliases and tags are not supported. The container is internal; consumer code receives services through constructor and hook parameters only.

Predefined services

Saij\WpAppFramework\Theme is a predefined instance in themes: Theme::boot() creates it (its constructor is private) and hands it to the container, which never builds it. Services can inject it to read the paths via getTemplateDirectory(), getTemplateDirectoryUri(), getStylesheetDirectory(), getStylesheetDirectoryUri() and getFrameworkDirectory().

In plugins, Saij\WpAppFramework\Plugin takes its place (getSlug(), getFile(), getDirectory(), getDirectoryUri(), getFrameworkDirectory()).

In child themes, Saij\WpAppFramework\ChildTheme (getSlug(), getParentSlug(), getDirectory(), getDirectoryUri(), getParentDirectory(), getParentDirectoryUri(), getFrameworkDirectory()).

Injecting the one of another kind is a build error.

Saij\WpAppFramework\Twig\TemplateRenderer is predefined as well; the framework creates it on first use (see Twig templates).

title: Twig templates
description: Templates live in the src/ directory of each level, next to the code that uses them (src/Hook/Mail.twig) or in shared directories (src/Component/Button.twig). A template name is always the full path relative to src/, including the extension – in PHP and in templates alike; there are no relative names.

title: Values
content:
Block attribute classes, nested value classes and #[ListOf] REST arguments share one schema derivation (build) and one value factory (runtime, without reflection).

Value class: a readonly class whose values are all public promoted constructor parameters and that declares no other properties. Value classes are the exception to the rule that properties are never public.

Types: int, float, string, bool, backed enums (schema enum with the case values), value classes (schema object with properties) and array with #[ListOf(Enum::class)] or #[ListOf(ValueClass::class)] (schema array with items), each optionally nullable (type: [..., 'null']). Lists of scalars are not supported yet. Enums and value classes must be in the scanned PSR-4 directories; recursive value classes are build errors.

Defaults become the schema default (enums as their value, value objects as arrays). Inside a nested value class a parameter without default is required. Unknown keys in nested objects are ignored, like WordPress ignores unknown block attributes.

#[Url] on a string adds format: uri (sanitized with sanitize_url()).

Conversion: missing values use the constructor default; a value that does not match its type throws an InvalidArgumentException naming the path, e.g. buttons[1].url – values are never coerced silently.

See Blocks and REST routes for how blocks and routes use them.

title: wp-app-framework
content:
PHP/JS framework for building standalone full site editing themes, child themes and plugins for WordPress 7 (PHP 8.5).

Composer package: saij/wp-app-framework

PHP namespace: Saij\WpAppFramework

JS import name: @saij/wp-app-framework, runtime global: window.wpAppFramework[slug] (one per framework instance)

Source: github.com/saijsaij/wp-app-framework

The framework is a library that themes, child themes and plugins (its consumers) include via Composer. It is neither a theme nor a plugin and registers no blocks itself. Each consumer runs its own framework instance; everything global – REST route, script handles, JS global, cache directory, init action – is named after the consumer's slug (its directory name), so a theme and several plugins with different framework versions run side by side.

Principles

No markup in post content. Every block renders on the server. The post content holds block comments with JSON attributes; block supports are attributes too. The only exception is one #[RichText(postContent: true)] field per block (see Blocks).

Inline editing in the editor canvas. Markup exists once, in Twig; the editor replaces the marked elements with editors (see Editor).

Full site editing. Pages are block templates and template parts. Twig renders block markup and markup fragments of your code (mails, HTML responses), never page layouts.

Plain WordPress. Releases ship all dependencies prefixed; the server needs neither Composer nor Bedrock (see Release).

Compiled in the build, not at runtime. Attributes such as #[Hook], #[RestRoute] and #[Block] are read by a build step that writes a manifest of plain data; a release loads it without reflection (see Boot and modes).

Status

The framework is in development (0.x); breaking changes are listed in Upgrading.

Framework core: boot, container, manifest build, development mode and #[Hook].

REST routes: #[RestController], #[RestRoute], #[Param].

Twig: TemplateRenderer, #[TemplateFunction], #[TemplateFilter].

Server-side blocks: #[Block], #[Supports], typed attribute classes, #[ListOf] also for REST arguments.

Editor runtime: inline editing in the canvas, generated inspector, batch render route, webpack helper.

Release: wp-app-framework release (prefixed ZIP), release mode with a versioned Twig cache, GitHub workflows.

Plugins: Plugin::boot(), theme overrides of plugin templates, public APIs and public template callables of plugins.

Child themes: ChildTheme::boot(), overrides of theme templates in overrides/{theme}/, public APIs and template callables of themes, #[ThemeApi].

Where to start

Getting started sets up a theme with a first block.

The guides describe each part of the API; Values is shared by blocks and REST routes.

A complete example of every feature is the test theme theme-dev-test, with the test plugin plugin-dev-test and the test child theme theme-dev-test-child.

A local WordPress for development is provided by wp-dev-env.

title: Upgrading
content:
Within a major version the consumer API only grows: nothing is renamed, removed or changed in behavior. Before 1.0, minor versions may break it; such changes are listed here.

The documentation is published per minor version; the version switcher in the navigation bar shows the documentation of other versions.

0.3

Child themes override theme templates in overrides/{theme}/ instead of src/ (see Twig templates). The src/ of a child theme belongs to its own framework instance (ChildTheme::boot(), see Child themes).

0.2

The init action is named after the consumer: wp_app_framework/init/{slug} instead of wp_app_framework/init (see Boot and modes).
